0.4 Distributions and Statistical Inference

From scenario tables to the normal distribution

Section titled “From scenario tables to the normal distribution”

In the scenario tables of 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance, a return could take only a few values. Real returns can be any number. If you draw a histogram of many years of returns and make the bars narrower and narrower, it approaches a smooth curve, the probability density. The area under the curve over an interval is the probability that the return falls in that interval; the area under the whole curve is 1.

The most common one is the normal distribution, written N(μ,σ2)N(\mu, \sigma^2)N(μ,σ2): bell-shaped, symmetric, and fully determined by its mean μ\muμ and standard deviation σ\sigmaσ. A useful rule:

RangeProbability of falling in the range
μ±1σ\mu \pm 1\sigmaμ±1σabout 68%
μ±2σ\mu \pm 2\sigmaμ±2σabout 95%
μ±3σ\mu \pm 3\sigmaμ±3σabout 99.7%

Example: an asset’s annual return follows N(8%,16%2)N(8\%, 16\%^2)N(8%,16%2). In about 68% of years the return is between −8% and 24%, and in about 95% of years between −24% and 40%. The remaining 5% is split equally between the two sides, so about one year in 40 has a loss deeper than −24%.

The number of standard deviations a value is from the mean is its z-score:

z=R−μσz = \frac{R - \mu}{\sigma}z=σR−μ​

For example, for a return of −24%, z=−24−816=−2z = \frac{-24 - 8}{16} = -2z=16−24−8​=−2. Every normal distribution becomes N(0,1)N(0, 1)N(0,1) after standardizing, so one table of the standard normal distribution gives all such probabilities.

Check C1
Annual returns follow N(8%,16%2)N(8\%, 16\%^2)N(8%,16%2). What is the approximate probability that a year's return is below −8%? Above 40%?

Fat tails

Section titled “Fat tails”

In real daily and monthly returns, extreme rises and falls occur more often than a normal distribution with the same standard deviation predicts. This is called fat tails. A fat-tailed distribution is usually more peaked in the middle and thicker in the tails.

Later in this course we still often use the normal distribution, because it is simple, its error is small for annual returns, and many conclusions do not depend on normality. But whenever a question involves extreme events, keep this limit in mind (4.13 Simulation and Backtesting Methods (not yet published)).

Check C2
On October 19, 1987, the US stock market fell about 20% in one day. Assume that the standard deviation of daily returns was then about 1% and the mean daily return about 0. Under a normal distribution, how many standard deviations from the mean is this event? Does the normal model consider such an event likely or unlikely? It did happen; what does that show? If a risk model assumes normally distributed returns, will its probability of a large fall be too high or too low?

Mean and median

Section titled “Mean and median”

You invest 100 dollars and flip a coin each year: heads, your wealth is multiplied by 1.5 (+50%); tails, by 0.6 (−40%). You play for 10 years.

Imagine 1,024 people (2102^{10}210), each playing independently with 100 dollars for 10 years. With 1,024 people, each sequence of heads and tails occurs exactly once, in line with its probability. There are now two different questions:

  • How much money does this group have per person on average? Add up everyone’s money and divide by 1,024. This is the expected value (expected value), also called the mean.
  • What is the result for a typical person? Line up the 1,024 people from least to most wealth; the wealth of the person in the middle is the median.

The two answer different questions, and they can be far apart:

Number of headsPeopleWealth per person (dollars)Share of total wealth
1015,7663.5%
9102,30713.8%
84592324.9%
712036926.6%
621014818.6%
5252598.9%
4210243.0%
3 or fewer176under 90.8%

The mean is about 162.9 dollars (equal to 100×1.0510100 \times 1.05^{10}100×1.0510), and the median is 59.0 dollars (5 heads, 5 tails). Only the 176 people with 7 or more heads (17%) are above the mean, yet they hold 69% of the total wealth; the 638 people who end with a loss (62%) hold only 13%.

Why does the mean rise while the median falls?

  • For the whole group: each year, each person’s money is multiplied by 1.5+0.62=1.05\frac{1.5 + 0.6}{2} = 1.0521.5+0.6​=1.05 on average, so the mean is 100×1.05n100 \times 1.05^n100×1.05n.
  • For a typical person: about half the years are heads and half tails. One head and one tail together give 1.5×0.6=0.91.5 \times 0.6 = 0.91.5×0.6=0.9, so the median is about 100×0.9n/2100 \times 0.9^{n/2}100×0.9n/2.

There is no contradiction. Money grows and shrinks in proportion: for the lucky people the base keeps growing, so +50% adds more and more dollars; for the unlucky people the base keeps shrinking, so −40% takes away fewer and fewer dollars, and they can lose at most almost everything. Almost all the growth of total wealth comes from a few lucky people. Losses have a floor and gains have no ceiling, so the distribution has a long tail on the right that pulls the mean above the median. This is called right skew.

Optional. The logarithm of wealth is the sum of the yearly log returns (log return):

ln⁡Wn=ln⁡W0+∑t=1nln⁡(1+Rt)\ln W_n = \ln W_0 + \sum_{t=1}^{n} \ln(1 + R_t)lnWn​=lnW0​+t=1∑n​ln(1+Rt​)

With many years, this sum is approximately normal, so wealth approximately follows a lognormal distribution. If ln⁡Wn\ln W_nlnWn​ has mean mmm and standard deviation sss, the median of wealth is eme^mem and its mean is em+s2/2e^{m + s^2/2}em+s2/2: the more volatile the returns and the more years, the further apart the two are. Wealth invested in stocks works the same way, though the gap is smaller than in this example (4.1 Measuring Return and Risk (not yet published)).

Check C3
The same coin-flip investment (each year the wealth is multiplied by 1.5 or 0.6 with equal probability), starting with 100 dollars, for 2 years. What are the possible outcomes and their probabilities? What are the mean wealth and the median?

Estimating from data: sample mean and sample standard deviation

Section titled “Estimating from data: sample mean and sample standard deviation”

The scenario tables in 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance assume that we know the probabilities, so the true μ\muμ and σ\sigmaσ can be computed directly; they are called population parameters. In reality we only have one stretch of historical data and must estimate them from it. This is parameter estimation. Estimates computed from data are called sample statistics:

  • the sample mean Rˉ\bar RRˉ, which estimates μ\muμ;
  • the sample standard deviation sss, which estimates σ\sigmaσ.

Example: a fund’s returns (%) over 5 years are 20, −5, 15, 30 and −10.

Step 1, the sample mean:

Rˉ=20−5+15+30−105=10\bar R = \frac{20 - 5 + 15 + 30 - 10}{5} = 10Rˉ=520−5+15+30−10​=10

Step 2, subtract the sample mean from each year to get the deviations, and square them:

YearReturn RtR_tRt​Deviation Rt−RˉR_t - \bar RRt​−RˉSquared deviation
12010100
2−5−15225
315525
43020400
5−10−20400
Total01,150

Step 3, divide the sum of squared deviations by n−1=4n - 1 = 4n−1=4 to get the sample variance, and take the square root to get the sample standard deviation:

s2=1n−1∑t=1n(Rt−Rˉ)2=11504=287.5,s=287.5≈16.96s^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{t=1}^{n} (R_t - \bar R)^2 = \frac{1150}{4} = 287.5, \qquad s = \sqrt{287.5} \approx 16.96s2=n−11​t=1∑n​(Rt​−Rˉ)2=41150​=287.5,s=287.5​≈16.96

Compare with 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance: there, outcomes were weighted by probability; here, each year is one observation, so each year gets the same weight, but the divisor is n−1n - 1n−1, not nnn.

Why divide by n−1n - 1n−1? The deviations are measured from the sample mean Rˉ\bar RRˉ, not from the true μ\muμ. Rˉ\bar RRˉ is computed from these same 5 numbers and always sits exactly at their center, so on average the 5 numbers are closer to Rˉ\bar RRˉ than to the true μ\muμ. Dividing by nnn would systematically underestimate σ\sigmaσ; dividing by n−1n - 1n−1 corrects exactly for this.

Another way to see it: the deviations always add up to 0 (the last row of the table). Once you know 4 of them, the fifth is fixed, so only n−1=4n - 1 = 4n−1=4 of them are free to vary. This number is the degrees of freedom. When nnn is large, dividing by nnn or by n−1n - 1n−1 makes almost no difference; when nnn is small, the difference is clear (here, dividing by 5 gives 15.17 and dividing by 4 gives 16.96).

Check C4
An asset's returns over 4 years are 12%, −4%, 8% and 24%. Calculate the sample mean and the sample standard deviation.

Standard error and confidence intervals

Section titled “Standard error and confidence intervals”

The sample mean is itself random. Imagine 100 parallel histories: in each one, 20 years of returns are drawn from the same true distribution (μ=8%\mu = 8\%μ=8%, σ=16%\sigma = 16\%σ=16%), and each history computes its own Rˉ\bar RRˉ. These 100 values of Rˉ\bar RRˉ are not equal; some are 3%, some 13%, spread around the true 8%. We actually live in one of these histories and see only one Rˉ\bar RRˉ.

The standard deviation of these 100 values of Rˉ\bar RRˉ is the standard error (SE) of the sample mean. It answers the question: in another history, how much would the average return typically differ?

If the returns of different years are independent and all have variance σ2\sigma^2σ2, then by the formula for a linear combination in 0.3 Probability: Expectation, Variance, Covariance and Portfolio Variance (portfolio variance), with all weights equal to 1n\frac{1}{n}n1​ and all covariances 0:

Var(Rˉ)=n⋅1n2σ2=σ2n,SE(Rˉ)=σn\text{Var}(\bar R) = n \cdot \frac{1}{n^2}\sigma^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}, \qquad \text{SE}(\bar R) = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}Var(Rˉ)=n⋅n21​σ2=nσ2​,SE(Rˉ)=n​σ​

Example: with σ=16%\sigma = 16\%σ=16% and n=20n = 20n=20, SE=16/20≈3.58%\text{SE} = 16 / \sqrt{20} \approx 3.58\%SE=16/20​≈3.58%. In practice σ\sigmaσ is unknown, so the sample standard deviation is used instead: SE≈s/n\text{SE} \approx s / \sqrt{n}SE≈s/n​. In the 5-year example of the previous section, SE≈16.96/5≈7.58%\text{SE} \approx 16.96 / \sqrt{5} \approx 7.58\%SE≈16.96/5​≈7.58%.

Confidence intervals. By the central limit theorem, the average of many independent observations is approximately normally distributed. So Rˉ\bar RRˉ is approximately normal with center μ\muμ and standard deviation SE. By the rule in the first section, in about 95% of the parallel histories Rˉ\bar RRˉ falls within μ±1.96 SE\mu \pm 1.96\,\text{SE}μ±1.96SE (1.96 is the exact value behind “2 standard deviations”).

Turned around: in each history, draw an interval centered on that history’s own Rˉ\bar RRˉ:

Rˉ±1.96×SE\bar R \pm 1.96 \times \text{SE}Rˉ±1.96×SE

In about 95% of the histories, this interval covers the true μ\muμ. This is a 95% confidence interval. The exact statement is: if intervals are built this way, about 95 of 100 histories produce an interval that contains the true μ\muμ; we do not know whether our own history is one of the other 5.

Example: 20 years of data, σ=16%\sigma = 16\%σ=16% and a sample mean of 8% give a 95% confidence interval of about [1.0%,15.0%][1.0\%, 15.0\%][1.0%,15.0%]. With 20 years of data, the error in the estimated average return is about plus or minus 7 percentage points.

Small samples. When sss replaces σ\sigmaσ, sss has its own error, so with a small sample the interval should be wider. The exact method replaces 1.96 with a critical value of the t distribution: about 2.78 for n=5n = 5n=5, about 2.09 for n=20n = 20n=20, and close to 1.96 for large nnn. The calculations in this course use 1.96 unless a question says otherwise.

Hypothesis tests

Section titled “Hypothesis tests”

A strategy had a positive average return in the past. Does that show that its true expected return is above 0? A hypothesis test answers questions like this: first assume that the true mean is 0 (the null hypothesis H0H_0H0​: μ=0\mu = 0μ=0), then check whether the data clearly contradict this assumption.

The number of standard errors that the sample mean is from 0 is the t-statistic:

t=RˉSEt = \frac{\bar R}{\text{SE}}t=SERˉ​

If μ\muμ really is 0, the probability that ∣t∣>1.96|t| > 1.96∣t∣>1.96 is only about 5%. So when ∣t∣>1.96|t| > 1.96∣t∣>1.96, the result is said to have statistical significance at the 5% level. Equivalently, the 95% confidence interval does not contain 0.

Example: in the 20-year example of the previous section, t=8/3.58≈2.24>1.96t = 8 / 3.58 \approx 2.24 > 1.96t=8/3.58≈2.24>1.96, which is significant at the 5% level.

Significance has limits:

  • Significant does not mean important: with a very large sample, even a tiny difference is significant.
  • Not significant does not mean the true value is 0: there may simply be too little data, so the interval is too wide.
  • Even a completely useless strategy has about a 5% chance of being significant by luck in each test. Testing many strategies and reporting only the significant ones is the problem of multiple testing (4.9 Performance Evaluation (not yet published)). What it leads to is for you to analyze in Exercises Question 6.
Check C8
A fund manager has beaten the index in each of the past 4 years. Does this show stock-picking skill? What more information is needed to judge?

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • A normal distribution is determined by μ\muμ and σ\sigmaσ: the probabilities within μ±1σ\mu \pm 1\sigmaμ±1σ, ±2σ\pm 2\sigma±2σ and ±3σ\pm 3\sigma±3σ are about 68%, 95% and 99.7%. Real returns have fat tails.
  • The mean is the average over a group; the median is the person in the middle. When wealth grows and shrinks in proportion and losses have a floor, the distribution is right-skewed and the mean is above the median.
  • Sample standard deviation: divide the sum of squared deviations by n−1n - 1n−1 and take the square root.
  • The standard error is how much the sample mean typically differs in another history, about s/ns / \sqrt{n}s/n​; the 95% confidence interval is Rˉ±1.96 SE\bar R \pm 1.96\,\text{SE}Rˉ±1.96SE.
  • ∣t∣>1.96|t| > 1.96∣t∣>1.96 means significance at the 5% level; significance has limits, and testing many hypotheses at once needs special care.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
Determine whether this statement is true or false, and explain: the more years of historical data you collect, the smaller the standard deviation of a stock's yearly return becomes.
Question 2
Explain: why is it too optimistic to look only at the "expected final wealth" when planning for retirement over a long period? What should the plan look at instead?
Question 3
Annual returns are normally distributed with μ=7%\mu = 7\%μ=7% and σ=15%\sigma = 15\%σ=15%. What is the approximate probability of a loss in a given year? (For the standard normal distribution, P(Z<−0.47)≈0.32P(Z < -0.47) \approx 0.32P(Z<−0.47)≈0.32.)
Question 4
An investment returns +60% or −40% each year with equal probability. (a) What is the expected return per year? (b) Starting with 100 dollars, what are the mean and the median wealth after 20 years? (c) Explain why they differ so much.
Question 5
A fund manager has beaten the index by an average of 3 percentage points a year over the past 5 years, and the yearly standard deviation of the outperformance is 6 percentage points. Use the standard error and the t-statistic to judge: does this show skill at the 5% level?
Question 6
A researcher tested 20 unrelated stock-picking strategies and reports that 1 of them is "significant at the 5% level". What do you make of this? What if 100 strategies had been tested?
